css-reorder-changes-meaning-vs-harmless: CSS positions content in a different order than the HTML source, so a screen reader (which follows source order) reads it in a nonsensical sequence.
layout-table-linearization-scrambles-seq: A layout table looks right as a grid, but read cell-by-cell it interleaves and shreds the text, so a screen-reader user hears a scrambled, meaningless sequence.
whitespace-within-word-vs-initialism: Letters of a single word are spaced apart for visual effect, so a screen reader reads it letter-by-letter rather than as the word it spells.
faked-columns-tables-in-plain-text: Columns or a table are faked with spaces and line breaks inside preformatted text, so a screen reader reads straight across them and interleaves the parts into gibberish.
responsive-breakpoint-order-desync: At one screen size CSS reorders items (stacking wizard steps as 2,1,3 on mobile), so the visual order no longer matches the source order a screen reader reads.
bidi-rtl-source-order-vs-visual: In mixed left-to-right and right-to-left text, an author physically reorders characters to look right on screen, so a screen reader hears them in the wrong logical order.
applicability-and-multiple-valid-orders: Deciding when order even matters: two unrelated articles can appear in either order safely, so flagging a page just because blocks could be reordered would be wrong.
